title: Desktop app
summary: Commonplace: the book is written and read in a Tauri app on phone and desktop.
description: A local-first app holds the book, so it works offline and the data stays on the author's devices. It is called Commonplace, after the commonplace book: a personal book of what one finds worth keeping, added to for a lifetime.

requirements.text: The product is a Tauri app.
The app runs on every platform in `app.platforms`.
The app is called `app.name` and shows the logo in the figure as its icon and in its sidebar.
The app has a light and a dark theme, made of the `color.*` values; it follows the system's setting unless the author picks one, on each device.
A change between the light and the dark theme animates over `theme.transition`, whoever made it; when the system asks for reduced motion, it switches at once.
The book's text is set in `font.book`, and the app's own interface in `font.ui`, both bundled with the app.
From any screen, `Ctrl+K` (`⌘K` on macOS) opens a search that jumps to any page.

Settings holds only rows: each opens a page nested in it (`/settings/ai` for the OpenRouter key and the models, `/settings/sync`, `/settings/costs`) or another screen, and says in a line how that part stands; a setting that is a single switch sits in its row. Each nested page leads back to Settings.

history.text: Settings is a page of rows, each opening a page nested in it, `/settings/sync` and `/settings/costs` among them; each row says in a line how that part stands, and each nested page leads back to Settings.
history.reason: The OpenRouter key and the models still sat on Settings itself, under its rows; the author wants Settings to be rows leading into sub-pages and nothing more.

requirements.text: How a part of the app works is explained behind an info button beside it, not in the screen's text; the screen's text says how things stand.

Every screen has an address, and the address also holds what the screen shows within it: where it's scrolled to, and what's chosen, searched or filtered there. Opening the address shows the same thing at the same place.
Keeping the address current while the author scrolls or chooses replaces it instead of adding a step, so going back leaves the screen.
Lists offer no deleting: a thing is deleted from its own screen, behind its menu (⋯), and asks first.
